en.title: Science Laboratory Technology: the whole course
en.short: What laboratory science covers, how the awards are organised, and how to study and practise it well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Science Laboratory Technology is the study of how to carry out reliable laboratory work and how to run a laboratory. It brings together chemistry, physics, biology and mathematics, then applies them to the analysis of samples: blood, water, food, soil, drugs and industrial products.

The subject matters because laboratory results drive decisions. A patient may be treated, a water supply declared safe, or a food batch released on the strength of a number a technician produced. Good technique, honest recording and quality control protect those decisions.

These summaries teach principles and standard practice. They do not replace your laboratory manual, your institution’s safety rules or the current standard for a test. Standards differ by country and change over time, so check the current official document.

sections.heading: How the course is usually organised
sections.text:
Programmes differ by country and institution, so read your own handbook for the exact structure, duration and award.

In Nigeria, polytechnics commonly offer a two-year National Diploma (ND), then industrial training, then a two-year Higher National Diploma (HND). Universities offer a Bachelor of Science, commonly four years, and many courses include industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. In the United Kingdom a foundation degree or BSc usually takes two to three years, and a sandwich year adds a year of placement. Ghana, Kenya and other countries have their own patterns.

Most programmes begin with shared science and laboratory practice, then move to analytical, biomedical, environmental and industrial analysis, and end with a project. A master’s degree adds advanced techniques and a dissertation. Check whether your award is accredited, and by which body, because this affects registration and practice.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage gives you the tools. Laboratory safety and good laboratory practice come first, because every later practical depends on them. Then laboratory mathematics, measurement and data handling; general chemistry, physics and biology; glassware, equipment and basic techniques; basic organic chemistry; introduction to analytical chemistry; and scientific communication and records.

The core stage carries the professional skills. Volumetric and gravimetric analysis and separation techniques, including chromatography, come next, followed by instrumental analysis and spectroscopy, then electrochemistry, potentiometry and conductometry. Organic synthesis and purification, and inorganic chemistry of salts and complexes, deepen the chemistry. The biomedical group covers biochemistry and clinical chemistry, microbiology, immunology and serology, haematology and blood banking, histology and cytology, and parasitology and medical entomology. Environmental and water analysis, and industrial and food analysis, apply the same skills to other samples. Quality assurance and method validation, laboratory management and ethics, and research methods with the final-year project complete the stage.

At master’s level, advanced analytical chemistry and trace analysis, molecular biology and biotechnology, advanced biomedical laboratory science, and a dissertation build on that base.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Practise with your hands. A technique is learned by repeating it: pipetting, titration, weighing, staining, streaking plates, calibrating a pH meter. Keep a bound notebook and write what you actually did, in ink, at the time, including mistakes.

Learn the reason behind each step. Why is a burette rinsed with the titrant and not with water? Why is a blank run? Why is a control included? When you can explain the purpose, you can adapt when something goes wrong.

Do calculations by hand until they are automatic, and carry units through every line. Judge results against plausible ranges. Read the method before the practical and write the report soon after.

sections.heading: Common mistakes

keyPoints: Laboratory results guide decisions about patients, water, food and products, so accuracy and honesty matter.
Safety and good laboratory practice come first because every later technique depends on them.
Course length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook and accreditation.
Learn the purpose behind each step, not only the sequence of actions.
Record data at the time, in ink, with units, and never adjust a result to fit expectation.
Quality control and method validation are part of the work, not an optional extra.

en.title: Laboratory safety and good laboratory practice
en.short: Hazards, risk assessment, PPE, safe handling, fire, waste, incidents and GLP.

sections.heading: Hazards and risk
sections.text:
A hazard is anything with potential to cause harm: chemicals, micro-organisms, sharps, heat, electricity, glassware and compressed gas. Risk is the chance that harm occurs and how serious it would be. Risk assessment identifies the hazard, who may be harmed, likelihood and severity, controls and responsibilities.

Controls follow a hierarchy: remove the hazard, substitute something safer, use engineering controls such as fume cupboards, then administrative controls such as standard operating procedures (SOPs), and only then personal protective equipment (PPE). Record and review when work changes.

sections.heading: PPE and handling
sections.text:
PPE includes a laboratory coat, safety glasses and suitable gloves. Choose gloves that resist the chemical concerned; no glove protects against everything. Wear PPE as the last barrier, not the first.

Before using a chemical, read the label and safety data sheet (SDS), work in a fume cupboard for volatile or toxic substances, and never pipette by mouth. Store incompatible chemicals apart. Treat all biological material as potentially infectious. Work at the correct containment level, disinfect surfaces, use sharps safely, and decontaminate waste by an approved method.

sections.heading: Fire, electricity, waste
sections.text:
Keep flammable liquids away from flames and sparks, know fire exits and extinguisher types, and never use water on live electrical equipment. Check leads and plugs for damage, keep water away from sockets, and switch off equipment before cleaning.

Waste must be segregated at source: chemical, biological, sharps and general. Put sharps in rigid sharps containers. Never pour chemicals down the sink unless local rules and your supervisor allow it.

sections.heading: Incidents and GLP
sections.text:
Report all incidents, including spills, injuries, exposures and near misses, to your supervisor and record them. A near miss could have caused harm. Reporting allows correction and prevents repetition.

Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) is a quality system: it requires trained staff, written SOPs, calibrated equipment, controlled records and independent audit. Formal GLP, as defined by the OECD, applies to non-clinical safety studies; teaching labs should copy these habits. Follow your institution’s current safety rules, which vary by country.

keyPoints: A hazard is a potential source of harm; risk is the chance and severity of harm.
Control measures follow a hierarchy of controls, with PPE as the last barrier.
Read labels and safety data sheets, and store incompatible chemicals apart.
Treat biological material as infectious and decontaminate waste by an approved method.
Segregate waste at source and report all incidents, including near misses.
Good Laboratory Practice is a quality system based on SOPs, training, records and audit.

en.title: Laboratory mathematics, measurement and data handling
en.short: SI units, significant figures, concentration, dilutions, calibration graphs and uncertainty.

sections.heading: Units and notation
sections.text: SI base units include metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Prefixes scale them: kilo (k) 10³, milli (m) 10⁻³, micro (µ) 10⁻⁶, nano (n) 10⁻⁹. Use consistent units throughout a calculation, then attach the correct unit to the answer. Scientific notation writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10; for example 0.00450 m = 4.50 × 10⁻³ m. This removes ambiguous zeros.

sections.heading: Significant figures
sections.text: All non-zero digits are significant. Zeros between them are significant; leading zeros are not; trailing zeros after a decimal point are. In multiplication and division, keep the least number of significant figures. In addition and subtraction, keep the least number of decimal places. Round only the final answer. Rounding rules vary slightly at exactly 5; state your convention and keep it consistent. Example: 12.34 × 0.50 = 6.17, but to two significant figures it is 6.2.

sections.heading: Concentration and dilution
sections.text: Mass percent = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100. Concentration in mol/dm³ = amount of solute (mol) ÷ volume of solution (dm³). Convert cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000. Dilution: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂. Example: dilute 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ to 250.0 cm³. C₂ = (0.200 × 25.0) ÷ 250.0 = 0.0200 mol/dm³.

sections.heading: Data and uncertainty
sections.text: A calibration graph plots instrument signal against standard concentration. Draw the best straight line and read unknown concentrations from it. Mean x̄ = Σx ÷ n. Sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]. Report results as mean ± s, with n and units, for example 10.3 ± 0.1 mg/L (n = 3). State the uncertainty source and avoid claiming more precision than the data support.

keyPoints: Use consistent units throughout a calculation; kilo = 10³, milli = 10⁻³, micro = 10⁻⁶, nano = 10⁻⁹.
Scientific notation is a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.
For × and ÷ keep least significant figures; for + and − keep least decimal places.
Mass percent = (mass solute ÷ mass solution) × 100; concentration (mol/dm³) = mol ÷ dm³.
Dilution: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.
Mean x̄ = Σx ÷ n; sample standard deviation s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]; report mean ± s with n and units.

en.title: General chemistry for laboratory science
en.short: Atomic structure, periodic trends, bonding, moles, acids and bases, redox, rates and equilibrium.

sections.heading: Atoms and periodicity
sections.text:
An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. Atomic number Z is the number of protons; mass number A is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A. Outer electrons determine chemistry.

Across a period, rising nuclear charge pulls electrons closer, so atoms get smaller and hold electrons more tightly. Down a group, extra shells make atoms larger and they lose electrons more easily. Flame tests give lithium crimson, sodium yellow.

sections.heading: Bonding and moles
sections.text:
Ionic bonds form when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal, as in NaCl. Covalent bonds form when atoms share electrons, as in H2O. Metallic bonding is positive ions in a sea of electrons.

One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant. Molar mass M is the mass of one mole in g/mol. Moles n = m ÷ M. Stoichiometry uses mole ratios from a balanced equation.

Example: 0.25 mol NaCl. M = 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol. m = 0.25 × 58.5 = 14.6 g.

sections.heading: Acids, bases, salts
sections.text:
A Brønsted-Lowry acid donates a proton (H⁺); a base accepts one. Strong acids such as HCl ionise completely in water; weak acids such as acetic acid ionise partly. pH = −log10[H⁺], so 0.01 M HCl has pH = 2.

An acid plus a base gives a salt plus water: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. In a titration, a burette delivers NaOH to a measured volume of HCl with phenolphthalein; the end point is a faint pink.

sections.heading: Redox, rates, equilibrium
sections.text:
Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain (OIL RIG). In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc is oxidised and copper(II) ions are reduced. The oxidising agent accepts electrons.

Reaction rate increases with concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts. At equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant. Le Chatelier’s principle predicts the shift when conditions change. In the lab, the iodine clock times a colour change to follow rate.

keyPoints: Atomic number Z is the number of protons; mass number A is protons plus neutrons, and isotopes differ only in A.
Across a period atoms get smaller and hold electrons more tightly; down a group they get larger and lose electrons more easily.
Ionic bonds transfer electrons, covalent bonds share them, and metallic bonding is positive ions in a sea of electrons.
Moles n = m ÷ M, one mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles, and stoichiometry uses mole ratios from a balanced equation.
pH = −log10[H⁺], and an acid plus a base gives a salt plus water.
Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain; at equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal.

en.title: General physics for laboratory science
en.short: Mechanics, heat, electricity, magnetism, waves and optics for laboratory instruments and measurement.

sections.heading: Forces and motion
sections.text: Mechanics explains how instruments hold, move and spin samples. Force is a push or pull; weight is the force of gravity on a mass, W = mg. A balance compares torques, not weights directly. Torque is force × perpendicular distance from a pivot. A centrifuge uses centripetal force F = mv² ÷ r to separate particles by density. Friction and stiffness affect moving parts, so calibration and levelling matter.

sections.heading: Heat and temperature
sections.text: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature measures average particle kinetic energy. A thermometer needs time to reach thermal equilibrium with a sample before its reading is reliable. Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. Most solids expand when heated; in instruments, thermal expansion can change lengths and volumes, and thermostats use bimetallic strips. Insulation reduces heat loss in incubators and water baths.

sections.heading: Electricity and magnetism
sections.text:
Electric current is charge flow, measured in amperes. Ohm’s law gives V = IR, where V is potential difference in volts, I current in amperes and R resistance in ohms. Power is P = VI. Meters must be connected correctly: an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel. Magnetic fields arise from currents and magnets; they drive motors, relays and magnetic stirrers.

Example: a 12 V supply across 240 Ω gives I = 12 ÷ 240 = 0.05 A (50 mA) and P = 12 × 0.05 = 0.6 W.

Electrical safety: earth metal cases, use fuses or circuit breakers, keep water away, and switch off and unplug before repair.

sections.heading: Waves and optics
sections.text: Waves carry energy; for any wave v = fλ, where v is speed, f frequency and λ wavelength. Light refracts when it changes speed between media; refractive index n = c ÷ v, where c is the speed of light in a vacuum and v is the speed of light in the medium. Lenses form images by refraction. On an optical bench, mount lamp, object, lens and screen on one rail, align their centres, and move the screen to the sharpest image. Record distances and repeat readings. Magnification = image height ÷ object height.

keyPoints: Weight is W = mg; torque is force × perpendicular distance.
Ohm’s law is V = IR and electrical power is P = VI.
Connect an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel.
For waves, v = fλ; refractive index is n = c ÷ v.
On an optical bench, align the components and focus for the sharpest image before measuring.
Electrical safety: earth metal cases, use fuses or breakers, keep water away, and isolate before repair.

en.title: General biology: cells, tissues and organisms
en.short: Cell structure, division and genetics, animal and plant tissues, and microorganism classification for lab specimens.

sections.heading: Cells and organelles
sections.text: All living things are made of cells, and new cells come from existing cells (cell theory). Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, lack a nucleus. Eukaryotic cells, such as plant and animal cells, have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Mitochondria release energy; ribosomes make protein; chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; the vacuole stores sap. In the laboratory you examine cheek cells, onion epidermis and Elodea leaf. A wet mount with water and a cover slip shows cytoplasm and nucleus; onion and Elodea also show a cell wall. Iodine stains starch in plant cells; methylene blue stains nuclei.

sections.heading: Division and genetics
sections.text: Mitosis produces two identical diploid cells (two chromosome sets) for growth and repair. Meiosis produces four haploid gametes (one set) with genetic variation. A gene is a length of DNA that codes for a trait; alleles are different versions of a gene. Genotype is the allele pair; phenotype is the visible trait. In a cross Tt × Tt, each parent gives T or t. The offspring are 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, so 3 tall : 1 short. Check: four boxes in a Punnett square, three contain T.

sections.heading: Tissues
sections.text: Animal tissues are epithelial (covering), connective (bone, blood), muscle (movement) and nervous (signals). Plant tissues include meristem (growth), parenchyma (storage), xylem (water) and phloem (food). Prepared slides of epithelium, blood smear and muscle are common laboratory specimens. A plant stem cross-section shows xylem inside and phloem outside.

sections.heading: Microorganisms
sections.text: Microorganisms include bacteria (prokaryotes), fungi (yeast, moulds), protozoa and algae (eukaryotes), and viruses (acellular). Classification groups organisms by shared features and gives each a two-part binomial name, genus then species, written in italics. Laboratory specimens include agar plates with bacterial colonies, bread mould, pond water and fixed slides. Record colony shape, colour and edge; these are observable features, not identification tests.

keyPoints: Cell theory states that all living things are made of cells and new cells come from existing cells.
Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Mitosis gives two identical diploid cells; meiosis gives four haploid gametes.
A Tt × Tt cross gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio (1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt).
The four animal tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous; plant xylem carries water and phloem carries food.
Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a genus and species name, written in italics.

en.title: Laboratory glassware, equipment and basic techniques
en.short: Glassware and balances, pipetting, burettes, filtration, heating, cleaning and calibration checks.

sections.heading: Glassware and balances
sections.text:
Choose glassware by purpose. Volumetric flasks, pipettes and burettes measure volume accurately; beakers and conical flasks mix and hold, not measure. Borosilicate glass tolerates heat better than soda-lime glass. Read the bottom of the meniscus, the curved liquid surface, at eye level. Never heat volumetric glass.

A top-pan balance reads to about 0.01 g. An analytical balance reads to 0.1 mg or better and has a draught shield. Level it, set zero with an empty container, and weigh only cool objects.

sections.heading: Pipetting and burettes
sections.text:
A volumetric pipette delivers one fixed volume; a graduated pipette delivers a range. Rinse with the liquid, fill above the mark, then release to the mark with the tip touching the vessel. Do not blow out a pipette marked TD (to deliver) unless instructed.

A burette is a graduated tube with a stopcock (tap). Rinse, fill, remove the air bubble, and read at eye level. Touch the tip to the flask wall to remove the hanging drop.

Calibration: a 25.00 mL pipette delivers 24.94 g of water at 20 °C. With density 0.9982 g/mL, volume = 24.94 ÷ 0.9982 = 24.985 mL. Error = −0.015 mL, or −0.06%.

sections.heading: Filtration, heating and records
sections.text:
Filtration separates a solid from a liquid. Fold and wet the paper, pour down a glass rod, and match paper grade to particle size; use vacuum filtration for crystals or when speed matters, since very fine solids can clog or pass through paper. Heat with a Bunsen burner, water bath or mantle. Add boiling chips, and never heat a closed system or volumetric glass. Clean with detergent and brush, rinse with tap water then distilled water; clean glass drains in an unbroken film.

Check balances with certified masses. Check volumetric glass by weighing the water it delivers or contains, using water density at that temperature. Record date, instrument, temperature, mass, volume and deviation. Record raw readings, units, sample, method and initials. Do not erase; draw one line through an error and write the correction.

keyPoints: Volumetric glassware is for accurate volume; beakers and conical flasks are not.
Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level and never heat volumetric glass.
Set an analytical balance to zero with the empty container and weigh only cool objects.
Rinse a pipette or burette with the liquid and remove air bubbles before use.
Calibration volume = mass of water ÷ water density at that temperature; percentage error = (measured − expected) ÷ expected × 100.
Record raw readings, units and corrections at the time; never erase original data.

en.title: Basic organic chemistry: naming, groups and reactions
en.short: Naming, functional groups, isomerism and simple reactions of the main organic families.

sections.heading: Naming compounds
sections.text:
Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds. In IUPAC nomenclature, the international naming system, the name has a root for the longest carbon chain, a suffix for the main functional group, and prefixes for branches. Number the chain so the main group gets the lowest possible number.

Example: CH3CH(OH)CH3 is propan-2-ol. CH3CH(CH3)CH2OH is 2-methylpropan-1-ol.

Propane means three carbons, -ol an alcohol and 2- the OH position.

sections.heading: Functional groups
sections.text:
A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives a family its characteristic properties. Alkanes contain only C-C and C-H single bonds. Alkenes contain a C=C double bond. Alcohols contain an -OH group. Carbonyl compounds contain C=O: aldehydes have it at the end of a chain, ketones within the chain. Carboxylic acids contain -COOH. Amines contain -NH2, -NHR or -NR2, where R is an alkyl group.

The group controls solubility, boiling point and reactivity. For example, alcohols hydrogen-bond, so ethanol boils higher than the alkane ethane.

sections.heading: Isomerism
sections.text:
Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Structural isomers differ in the carbon chain, in the position of a group, or in the functional group. For C3H8O, the isomers include propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol and methoxyethane.

Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but a different spatial arrangement. Cis-trans isomers occur when each carbon of a C=C carries two different groups. Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images.

sections.heading: Reactions and mechanisms
sections.text:
A mechanism is a step-by-step account of bond breaking and forming, shown with curly arrows from an electron-rich site to an electron-poor site. Alkanes undergo free-radical substitution with halogens in UV light. Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition; ethene with HBr gives bromoethane, and Markovnikov’s rule predicts the major product with unsymmetrical alkenes: the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogens.

Alcohols are oxidised (primary to aldehyde then acid, secondary to ketone), dehydrated to alkenes, and esterified with carboxylic acids. Carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition. Carboxylic acids neutralise bases and form esters. Amines are basic and form amides with acyl chlorides.

Example: ethanol with acidified K2Cr2O7 gives ethanal, then ethanoic acid.

keyPoints: IUPAC names use the longest chain, a suffix for the main group and lowest locants.
Functional groups define families: alkenes C=C, alcohols OH, carbonyl C=O, carboxylic acids COOH, amines NH2.
Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in structure or spatial arrangement.
Alkanes react by free-radical substitution; alkenes by electrophilic addition.
Alcohols oxidise, dehydrate and esterify; carboxylic acids neutralise and esterify; amines are basic.
A mechanism is a stepwise description of bond breaking and forming shown with curly arrows.

en.title: Introduction to analytical chemistry
en.short: Qualitative vs quantitative analysis, sampling, solutions, standards, errors, volumetric and gravimetric principles.

sections.heading: Qualitative and quantitative
sections.text: Analytical chemistry answers two questions. Qualitative analysis asks what is present: it identifies sample components. Quantitative analysis asks how much is present: it measures the amount of a named substance, the analyte. The rest of the sample is the matrix. A flame test that turns yellow shows sodium is present (qualitative). A titration that finds 0.050 mol/dm³ of sodium hydroxide gives its concentration (quantitative). Both need representative sampling.

sections.heading: Sampling and solutions
sections.text:
Sampling takes a small portion that represents the whole bulk. A sample that is not representative makes every later result wrong. A solution is prepared by dissolving a known mass of solute and making the solution up to the mark in a volumetric flask. Molarity, c = n ÷ V, is moles of solute per cubic decimetre (dm³) of solution.

Worked example: prepare 250 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium carbonate (Na2CO3, M = 106.0 g/mol).
n = c × V = 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol
mass = n × M = 0.0250 × 106.0 = 2.65 g
Weigh 2.65 g, dissolve, and make up to 250 cm³.

sections.heading: Primary standards and errors
sections.text: A primary standard is a reagent pure enough, stable enough and of known formula to weigh directly and prepare a solution of accurately known concentration. Examples are potassium hydrogen phthalate and dried sodium carbonate. A secondary standard is standardised against a primary standard. Errors are systematic (a constant bias, such as a miscalibrated balance) or random (unpredictable scatter). Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated results to each other.

sections.heading: Volumetric and gravimetric
sections.text: Volumetric analysis measures the volume of a solution of known concentration that reacts completely with the analyte. In a titration the equivalence point is reached when the amounts react in the stoichiometric ratio; an indicator signals the end point. Gravimetric analysis converts the analyte into a solid of known composition, which is filtered, dried, and weighed. Its mass gives the amount of analyte. These principles are developed in the core course.

keyPoints: Qualitative analysis identifies what is present; quantitative analysis measures how much.
A representative sample is essential because a poor sample invalidates the whole analysis.
Molarity: c = n ÷ V, where n is moles and V is volume in dm³.
A primary standard is pure, stable and weighed directly; a secondary standard is standardised against it.
Systematic error is a constant bias; random error is unpredictable scatter.
Volumetric methods measure reacting volume; gravimetric methods weigh a solid of known composition.

en.title: Scientific communication and laboratory records
en.short: Keeping a lab notebook, writing reports, presenting tables and graphs, and citing sources without plagiarism.

sections.heading: The laboratory notebook
sections.text: A laboratory notebook is the primary record of your work. Use a bound book with numbered pages and write in ink. For each experiment record the date, aim, method, raw observations, calculations and conclusion as you go. If you make a mistake, draw one line through it, write the correction beside it and initial it. Never erase or tear out pages. A supervisor may sign and date the page as a witness. The notebook must be honest and complete because it shows what you actually did.

sections.heading: Reports, tables and graphs
sections.text: A report usually has a title, abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Write the method in the past tense with enough detail for another person to repeat the work. Put raw data in the results and interpretation in the discussion. Tables give exact numbers; number them above with units in the headings. Graphs show trends: independent variable on the x-axis, dependent on the y-axis, both axes labelled with units, caption below. Example: a student records the temperature of a cooling liquid every minute. The table lists time and temperature; the graph plots temperature against time and shows the cooling curve. Present data for the audience: full detail in a report, one clear graph on a poster, a simple slide in a talk.

sections.heading: Citing and plagiarism
sections.text: Cite every idea, fact or method that is not your own. A citation gives author, year and source; the format depends on your department’s style (for example, Harvard, APA or Vancouver). Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s words or ideas as your own. Avoid it by paraphrasing (restating in your own words) and citing the source, or by using quotation marks and a citation for a direct copy. Keep a reference list of everything you cite. Reusing your own past work without permission is also plagiarism. For different audiences, adjust jargon and detail but never change the data.

keyPoints: A laboratory notebook is a bound, numbered, ink record of date, aim, method, raw data and conclusion; correct mistakes with a single line and initials.
A report has a title, abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion, conclusion and references; write the method in the past tense so it can be repeated.
Put raw data in the results and interpretation in the discussion; state units and uncertainty.
Tables give exact numbers with units in headings; graphs put the independent variable on the x-axis and label both axes with units.
Cite every borrowed idea, fact or method in the style your department requires; paraphrasing still needs a citation.
Plagiarism includes copying words or ideas without credit and reusing your own past work without permission; adjust detail for the audience but never change the data.

en.title: Volumetric and gravimetric analysis
en.short: Titration types, indicators, primary standards, gravimetric procedure, calculations and errors.

sections.heading: Titration basics
sections.text: Volumetric analysis measures the volume of a standard solution, one of known concentration, that reacts completely with the analyte, the substance being measured. The equivalence point is the stoichiometric point; the end point is what the indicator shows. A primary standard is a very pure, stable, non-hygroscopic substance of high molar mass, such as potassium hydrogen phthalate for acid-base work or potassium dichromate for redox work. It is used to standardise a secondary solution. Indicators must change colour near the equivalence point, so their pH range or electrode potential must match the reaction.

sections.heading: Four titration types
sections.text: Acid-base titrations use neutralisation, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, with pH indicators such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange. Redox titrations transfer electrons; permanganate is self-indicating, while iodine-thiosulphate uses starch. Complexometric titrations use a ligand, usually EDTA, to bind metal ions; pH buffers and metal-ion indicators control the end point. Precipitation titrations form a sparingly soluble salt, as in chloride with silver nitrate using Mohr or adsorption indicators. Each method needs the correct stoichiometric ratio from the balanced equation.

sections.heading: Gravimetric analysis
sections.text: Gravimetric analysis converts the analyte into a pure, insoluble form that is filtered, washed, dried or ignited, and weighed. The precipitate must be coarse enough to filter, and its solubility loss must be small. Co-precipitation and post-precipitation carry impurities; peptisation loses precipitate. The gravimetric factor converts precipitate mass to analyte mass: mass analyte = mass precipitate × (M analyte ÷ M precipitate) × (moles analyte ÷ moles precipitate), where M is molar mass.

sections.heading: Calculation and error
sections.text: Example: 25.00 cm³ HCl needs 24.60 cm³ of 0.1000 mol/dm³ NaOH. NaOH moles = 0.1000 × 24.60 ÷ 1000 = 0.002460 mol. HCl moles equal this (1:1), so c(HCl) = 0.002460 ÷ (25.00 ÷ 1000) = 0.09840 mol/dm³. Main errors are burette and pipette calibration, parallax, temperature, indicator choice, reaction completeness, and, in gravimetry, impurity, loss and incomplete drying. Report results with uncertainty and check the method blank.

keyPoints: Volumetric analysis uses a standard solution of known concentration; the end point is observed and the equivalence point is stoichiometric.
A primary standard is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, of high molar mass and reacts stoichiometrically.
Acid-base, redox, complexometric and precipitation titrations each need a suitable indicator and a balanced equation.
Titration formula: moles = concentration × volume in dm³, and c1V1/n1 = c2V2/n2, where n1 and n2 are stoichiometric coefficients.
Gravimetric factor: mass analyte = mass precipitate × (M analyte ÷ M precipitate) × (moles analyte ÷ moles precipitate).
Main errors are calibration, parallax, temperature, indicator mismatch, incomplete reaction, co-precipitation and ignition loss.

en.title: Separation techniques and chromatography
en.short: Extraction, distillation, filtration, centrifugation, paper, TLC, column, gas and liquid chromatography.

sections.heading: Bulk methods
sections.text:
Solvent extraction shakes a solute between two liquids that do not mix. The solute distributes itself according to its partition coefficient, K = concentration in solvent 1 ÷ concentration in solvent 2. Like dissolves like, so a non-polar solute favours a non-polar solvent. Repeated small portions extract more than one large portion.

Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Simple distillation suits a volatile liquid from a non-volatile solute; fractional distillation uses a column and repeated evaporation and condensation for close boiling points.

Filtration separates a solid from a liquid by particle size. Centrifugation spins a sample; denser material forms a pellet and the liquid is the supernatant.

sections.heading: Planar chromatography
sections.text: Paper and thin layer chromatography (TLC) use a fixed stationary phase and a moving mobile phase. In paper chromatography the stationary phase is water held on cellulose; in TLC it is a thin layer of silica or alumina on a plate. A spot is applied, the plate is placed in solvent, and the solvent front rises by capillary action. Components move at different rates by partition or surface adsorption. The retention factor is Rf = distance travelled by spot ÷ distance travelled by solvent front. Example: a spot moves 3.0 cm and the front moves 8.0 cm, so Rf = 3.0 ÷ 8.0 = 0.375. Rf depends on the solvent and the stationary phase, so report the system.

sections.heading: Column methods
sections.text: Column chromatography packs a stationary phase in a tube. The mobile phase carries the mixture through; components with weaker retention leave the column first, and fractions are collected. Gas chromatography (GC) uses a carrier gas as mobile phase. A volatile, heat-stable sample is vaporised, carried through a heated column, and partitioned between gas and stationary phase before detection. Liquid chromatography (LC) uses a liquid mobile phase. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) pumps solvent through a column of fine particles at high pressure, giving sharp separations.

keyPoints: Partition coefficient K = concentration in solvent 1 ÷ concentration in solvent 2.
Distillation separates by boiling point; filtration by particle size; centrifugation by density.
Paper and TLC separate by partition or adsorption; Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent front distance.
Column chromatography collects fractions as the mobile phase carries components through.
Gas chromatography needs volatile, heat-stable samples and uses a carrier gas mobile phase.
Liquid chromatography uses a liquid mobile phase; HPLC uses high pressure and fine particles.

en.title: Instrumental analysis: spectroscopy
en.short: Absorption and emission, UV-visible, IR, AAS, flame emission, Beer-Lambert and calibration.

sections.heading: Absorption and emission
sections.text: Absorption occurs when a molecule or atom takes in a photon whose energy matches a transition from a lower to a higher energy level. Emission is the reverse: an excited species loses energy by emitting a photon. The photon energy is E = hν = hc ÷ λ, so shorter wavelength means higher energy. Absorption measures light removed; emission measures light given out.

sections.heading: UV visible and Beer-Lambert
sections.text:
UV-visible spectroscopy uses electronic transitions, usually in solution over about 200 to 800 nm. A chromophore is the part of a molecule that absorbs. Absorbance A = log10(I0 ÷ I), where I0 is incident and I is transmitted intensity. The Beer-Lambert law is A = ε c l: ε is molar absorptivity (L mol−1 cm−1), c is concentration (mol L−1) and l is path length (cm). It holds for dilute solutions and monochromatic (single-wavelength) light; high concentration or stray light causes deviation.

Example: a 1.00 cm cell gives A = 0.45 for c = 3.0 × 10−5 mol L−1.
ε = A ÷ (c l) = 0.45 ÷ (3.0 × 10−5 × 1.00) = 1.5 × 10⁴ L mol−1 cm−1.

sections.heading: Infrared and atomic methods
sections.text: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy uses vibrational transitions. Wavenumber is 1 ÷ λ, usually 4000 to 400 cm−1. IR identifies functional groups, for example a broad O-H stretch near 3200 to 3600 cm−1 or a C=O stretch near 1700 cm−1; it is less often used for routine concentration measurement. Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) atomises the sample in a flame or furnace and measures absorption by ground-state atoms at a resonance line from a hollow-cathode lamp. Flame emission (flame photometry) measures light emitted by excited atoms in a flame; it is useful for sodium, potassium and calcium. Both use calibration curves.

sections.heading: Calibration and spectra
sections.text: A calibration curve is made from standards of known concentration, a blank, and the instrument response. Plot response against concentration; the slope of a linear Beer-Lambert plot is εl. Use only the linear range. For simple spectra, read UV-visible λmax and band intensity, and IR peak position and shape. Emission lines identify elements; absorption bands identify electronic or vibrational environments.

keyPoints: Absorption needs photon energy matching a transition; emission is light from excited species.
Beer-Lambert law: A = ε c l, with A = log10(I0 ÷ I).
ε has units L mol−1 cm−1, c mol L−1 and l cm; use dilute solutions and single-wavelength light.
Calibration curves use standards and a blank; the linear slope is εl.
UV-visible shows electronic transitions; IR shows vibrational functional-group bands.
AAS measures absorption by atoms in a flame or furnace; flame emission measures atomic emission.

en.title: Electrochemistry, potentiometry and conductometry
en.short: Electrodes, pH and ion selective electrodes, potentiometric titrations, conductivity and applications.

sections.heading: Electrodes and cells
sections.text:
An electrochemical cell has two electrodes in an electrolyte. The indicator electrode responds to the analyte; the reference electrode keeps a stable potential, usually Ag/AgCl or calomel. Cell potential is Ecell = Ecathode − Eanode. The Nernst equation at 25 °C is E = E° − (0.0592 ÷ n) log10 Q, where Q uses activity (effective concentration).

Example: a glass electrode changes by about 59.2 mV per pH unit. If its potential falls 177.6 mV from pH 7 buffer, pH = 7 + 177.6 ÷ 59.2 = 10.0.

sections.heading: pH and ISEs
sections.text:
A pH meter measures the glass electrode potential against a reference. Calibrate with two buffers bracketing the sample, because slope and zero point drift; temperature affects slope.

An ion selective electrode (ISE) has a membrane giving a potential proportional to the log of one ion’s activity. The calibration graph is potential against log concentration. Other ions cause interference, described by selectivity. ISEs exist for fluoride, nitrate, calcium and ammonium. Standard addition helps with complex samples.

sections.heading: Potentiometric titrations
sections.text:
In a potentiometric titration the potential is measured after each titrant addition and plotted against volume. The equivalence point is the steepest part of the curve, found from the inflection or a Gran plot. It suits coloured or turbid samples where an indicator fails, and dilute solutions.

Example: chloride in water can be titrated with silver nitrate using a silver indicator electrode; the potential jump marks the end point.

sections.heading: Conductivity
sections.text:
Conductivity κ is a solution’s ability to carry current. Conductance G = 1 ÷ R. The cell constant k = distance ÷ area, so κ = G × k, in S/cm or S/m. Molar conductivity Λm = κ ÷ c. Strong electrolytes conduct well; weak ones depend on dissociation.

In conductometric titration, plot conductance against titrant volume; the equivalence point is where two straight lines meet. Example: R = 500 Ω gives G = 1 ÷ 500 = 0.002 S. If k = 1.25 cm⁻¹, κ = 0.002 × 1.25 = 0.0025 S/cm. Applications include checking water purity and controlling industrial streams.

keyPoints: Cell potential: Ecell = Ecathode − Eanode; the Nernst equation at 25 °C is E = E° − (0.0592 ÷ n) log10 Q.
A glass pH electrode responds by about 59.2 mV per pH unit at 25 °C, so calibration with buffers is essential.
An ion selective electrode gives a potential proportional to log activity; check selectivity and use standard addition if matrix effects are large.
In potentiometric titration, the equivalence point is the steepest part of the potential against volume curve.
Conductivity κ = G × cell constant, where G = 1 ÷ R; molar conductivity Λm = κ ÷ c.
Conductometric titration finds the equivalence point from the intersection of straight-line segments.

en.title: Organic reactions, synthesis and purification
en.short: Main functional group reactions, simple preparations, reflux, distillation, recrystallisation, melting points and yield.

sections.heading: Functional group reactions
sections.text: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition, for example with bromine water, which is decolourised, or with hydrogen halides. Alcohols are oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI): primary alcohols to aldehydes then carboxylic acids, secondary to ketones. They also dehydrate to alkenes and react with carboxylic acids to form esters. Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens’ reagent or Fehling’s solution; ketones are not. Carboxylic acids form esters with alcohols, and amides when heated with ammonia or amines. Amines are basic and are acylated by acid chlorides. Benzene rings undergo electrophilic substitution such as nitration and halogenation.

sections.heading: Preparations and reflux
sections.text: A simple preparation is ethyl ethanoate from ethanol and ethanoic acid with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid as catalyst. The mixture is heated under reflux: the vapour rises into a vertical condenser, condenses and returns to the flask. Reflux lets you heat for a long time without losing volatile reactants or solvent. After reflux, the ester is separated by distillation. Another preparation is a halogenoalkane from an alcohol and hydrogen halide.

sections.heading: Distillation and recrystallisation
sections.text: Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Simple distillation suits a volatile liquid from non-volatile impurities; fractional distillation separates liquids with close boiling points. Recrystallisation purifies a solid: dissolve it in the minimum of hot solvent, cool slowly so crystals form, then filter. Impurities stay in the cold solvent or are removed by hot filtration. The solvent must dissolve the compound well when hot and poorly when cold.

sections.heading: Yield, melting point and purity
sections.text: Percentage yield = (actual mass ÷ theoretical mass) × 100. Theoretical mass comes from the moles of the limiting reagent. Example: 23.0 g ethanol (0.500 mol) with excess ethanoic acid gives 35.2 g ethyl ethanoate. Molar mass of ethyl ethanoate is 88.1 g/mol, so theoretical mass = 0.500 × 88.1 = 44.05 g. Yield = 35.2 ÷ 44.05 × 100 = 79.9%. A pure solid melts sharply at its literature melting point; impurities lower and broaden the range. Purity is also checked by thin-layer chromatography, gas chromatography or spectroscopy.

keyPoints: Alkenes add electrophiles; alcohols oxidise, dehydrate and form esters; aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens’ reagent and Fehling’s solution, but ketones are not.
Reflux heats a mixture for a long time without losing volatile components.
Distillation separates by boiling point; recrystallisation purifies solids using hot solvent and slow cooling.
Percentage yield = (actual mass ÷ theoretical mass) × 100, using the limiting reagent for theoretical mass.
A pure solid has a sharp melting point; impurities lower and broaden it.
Purity can be checked by melting point, chromatography or spectroscopy.

en.title: Inorganic chemistry: salts, complexes and periodic trends
en.short: Salt preparation and solubility, qualitative ion tests, coordination compounds, oxidation states and periodic trends.

sections.heading: Salts and solubility
sections.text: A salt is an ionic compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. Prepare soluble salts from acid plus metal, oxide, hydroxide or carbonate, then crystallise; prepare insoluble salts by precipitation. For example, copper(II) sulfate is made from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid: CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O. Solubility rules guide the choice: nitrates and ammonium salts are soluble; most chlorides are soluble except silver and lead chlorides; most sulfates are soluble except barium, lead and calcium sulfates; most carbonates are insoluble except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates. Confirm exceptions.

sections.heading: Qualitative analysis
sections.text: Qualitative inorganic analysis identifies ions, not amounts. Flame tests give colours: sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium brick red, copper blue green. Cations are separated by controlled pH and precipitation with HCl, H2S, NaOH or NH3; anions are tested with AgNO3, BaCl2 and dilute acid. A precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia, such as AgCl, or a coloured complex, such as [Cu(NH3)4]2+, helps confirm the ion. Compare with known standards.

sections.heading: Coordination compounds
sections.text: A coordination compound contains a central metal ion bonded to ligands by coordinate bonds. The coordination number is the number of donor atoms. In [Cu(NH3)4]2+ the ligand is NH3, the coordination number is 4 and copper is +2. Oxidation state is found by adding the ligand charges: in [Fe(CN)6]3−, let iron be x; x + 6(−1) = −3, so x = +3. Complexes show colour, magnetism and isomerism; lab examples include deep blue [Cu(NH3)4]2+ and blood-red [Fe(SCN)]2+.

sections.heading: Periodicity in the lab
sections.text: Across a period, atomic radius falls and ionisation energy, electronegativity and non-metallic character rise; down a group, radius rises and ionisation energy falls. These trends explain lab behaviour: sodium reacts vigorously with water, magnesium slowly, and aluminium hardly at all because of its oxide layer. Oxides change from basic (Na2O) through amphoteric (Al2O3) to acidic (SO3). Oxidation states often follow group number, but transition metals show variable states, as in Fe2+ and Fe3+.

keyPoints: Soluble salts are prepared by acid-base or acid-carbonate reactions; insoluble salts by precipitation.
Solubility rules predict precipitates, but exceptions must be confirmed by qualitative tests.
Qualitative analysis identifies ions by flame colour, selective precipitation and confirmatory complex formation.
In a complex, the coordination number counts donor atoms and the oxidation state follows charge balance.
Across a period atomic radius falls while ionisation energy and electronegativity rise; down a group the reverse occurs.
Charge balance: metal oxidation state + sum of ligand charges = overall complex charge.

en.title: Biochemistry and clinical chemistry
en.short: Biomolecules, enzymes, metabolism and clinical measurement of glucose, proteins, lipids, electrolytes and organ markers.

sections.heading: Biomolecules and enzymes
sections.text: Biomolecules are the organic molecules of life: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; their shape determines function. Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy and are specific to substrates. Activity depends on pH, temperature, substrate concentration and inhibitors. Km is the substrate concentration at half of Vmax. Enzymes such as ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, amylase and lipase are measured because they leak from damaged tissue.

sections.heading: Metabolism and markers
sections.text: Metabolism is the sum of chemical reactions. Catabolism breaks molecules down and releases energy; anabolism builds them. Outline: glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate with net ATP; the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation produce most ATP; gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis maintain blood glucose; lipolysis releases fatty acids; the urea cycle removes ammonia; bilirubin comes from haem breakdown. Liver markers include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin. Kidney markers include creatinine, urea and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Electrolytes include sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate.

sections.heading: Clinical measurement
sections.text: Glucose is measured by glucose oxidase or hexokinase methods. Total protein uses the biuret reaction; albumin uses bromocresol green. Cholesterol uses cholesterol oxidase; triglycerides use enzymatic glycerol release. Electrolytes are measured by ion-selective electrodes or photometry. Liver and kidney markers use enzymatic or colorimetric assays. Creatinine clearance estimates kidney function: C = (U × V) ÷ (P × T), where U and P are urine and serum creatinine, V is urine volume and T is time. Example: U = 100 mg/dL, P = 1.0 mg/dL, V = 1500 mL, T = 1440 min. C = (100 × 1500) ÷ (1.0 × 1440) = 104 mL/min. Reference intervals vary with method and population.

sections.heading: Quality control
sections.text: Quality control protects results. Run calibrators and control materials. Internal QC uses Levey-Jennings charts and Westgard rules to detect random and systematic error. External quality assessment compares your results with other laboratories. Reference intervals depend on method and population, so each laboratory should verify them.

keyPoints: Enzymes are protein catalysts; Km is the substrate concentration at half of Vmax.
Metabolism includes catabolic and anabolic pathways; liver and kidney markers reflect organ function.
Glucose, protein, lipid and electrolyte assays use enzymatic, colorimetric or ion-selective methods.
Creatinine clearance: C = (U × V) ÷ (P × T); with U = 100 mg/dL, P = 1.0 mg/dL, V = 1500 mL and T = 1440 min, C = 104 mL/min.
Quality control uses calibrators, Levey-Jennings charts, Westgard rules and external quality assessment.
Reference intervals vary by method and population, so verify them locally.

en.title: Microbiology: sterilisation, culture and identification
en.short: Sterilisation, aseptic technique, media, inoculation, staining, culture and biochemical identification.

sections.heading: Sterilisation and asepsis
sections.text:
Sterilisation kills or removes all viable microorganisms, including spores. Disinfection reduces pathogens but may not kill spores. Autoclaving is usual for media and glassware; follow the validated cycle, typically 121 °C at about 15 psi. Dry heat suits metal and glass; filtration sterilises heat-labile liquids.

Aseptic technique keeps cultures pure. Work near a flame, flame loops and bottle necks, open vessels briefly, and never touch sterile surfaces. Example: Ada flames her loop before and after streaking a soil sample.

sections.heading: Media and inoculation
sections.text:
Culture media supply water, nutrients, salts and sometimes selective agents. Weigh accurately, dissolve in distilled water, adjust pH, dispense, then sterilise. Agar is a solidifying agent, not a nutrient. Cool molten agar to about 45 to 50 °C before adding heat-sensitive supplements. Label plates with medium, organism and date.

Inoculation introduces a sample into medium. Streak plating dilutes cells across agar to give separate colonies; spread plating distributes a liquid sample; stab and pour methods suit specific tests. Incubate at the temperature and atmosphere stated for the organism. A pure culture contains one organism; a contaminant is an unwanted one.

sections.heading: Staining and colonies
sections.text:
Staining makes cells visible and shows group differences. In the Gram stain, crystal violet stains all cells, iodine fixes the dye, alcohol decolourises Gram-negative cells, and safranin counterstains them. Gram-positive bacteria stay purple; Gram-negative bacteria appear pink or red. Timing and culture age affect results. Lactophenol cotton blue helps show fungal structures.

Colony characteristics include size, shape, margin, elevation, colour, opacity and consistency. Record them from well-isolated colonies on a plate. Fungal microscopy shows hyphae, spores and budding yeasts.

sections.heading: Biochemical identification
sections.text: Biochemical tests detect enzymes or metabolic pathways. Catalase and oxidase are quick tests; indole, citrate, urease, nitrate reduction and sugar fermentation help separate groups. Use pure cultures and compare with a known control. Identification combines colony appearance, microscopy, staining and biochemical results. No single test is enough. Results vary with medium, incubation and strain, so follow the laboratory protocol.

keyPoints: Sterilisation removes all viable microorganisms including spores; disinfection may not.
Aseptic technique and flaming loops prevent contamination and keep cultures pure.
Media must be correctly prepared, pH adjusted and sterilised; agar is not a nutrient.
Streak plating produces separate colonies for pure culture and identification.
Gram stain divides bacteria into purple Gram-positive and pink or red Gram-negative groups.
Identification uses colony appearance, microscopy, staining and biochemical tests together, not one test alone.

en.title: Immunology and serology: immunity, antibodies and diagnostic tests
en.short: Innate and adaptive immunity, antigens, antibodies, agglutination, precipitation, ELISA and serology quality control.

sections.heading: Innate and adaptive immunity
sections.text:
Innate immunity is the first line of defence: skin and mucous membranes, phagocytes, complement and inflammation. It acts quickly and has no memory.

Adaptive immunity is specific and has memory. B lymphocytes make antibodies, while T lymphocytes kill infected cells or help B cells. It takes days to develop. Active immunity follows infection or vaccination; passive immunity is borrowed antibody, such as maternal IgG across the placenta.

sections.heading: Antigens and antibodies
sections.text:
An antigen is any substance recognised by an antibody or T-cell receptor; an immunogen can provoke a response.

Antibodies are immunoglobulins made by plasma cells. IgG is the main antibody in blood and crosses the placenta; IgM is the first made in infection and agglutinates well; IgA is in secretions. Serology detects antibody or antigen in serum. A titre is the highest dilution that still gives a positive reaction.

sections.heading: Agglutination and precipitation
sections.text:
Agglutination clumps particulate antigens, such as red cells or latex beads. Precipitation forms a visible line or band when soluble antigen meets antibody in the right proportions. Prozone is antibody excess; postzone is antigen excess; both can cause false negatives.

Example: a serum titre of 1:160 means one part serum in 160 parts total. If 10 microlitres of serum is used, add 1,590 microlitres of diluent.

sections.heading: ELISA and quality control
sections.text:
ELISA uses an enzyme linked to an antibody or antigen; substrate produces colour proportional to bound label. In indirect ELISA, antigen is coated, patient antibody binds, then enzyme-labelled anti-human antibody detects it.

Sandwich ELISA detects antigen between capture and detection antibodies. Always include blank, negative and positive controls. Interpret only if controls are within limits. A reactive screening result may need confirmation by a second method, following the national algorithm. Quality control includes kit storage, incubation time and temperature, washing, calibration and recording lot numbers.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is specific and has memory.
IgG is the main antibody in blood and crosses the placenta; IgM appears first in infection and agglutinates well.
Agglutination uses particulate antigens, while precipitation uses soluble antigens.
Prozone and postzone are antibody and antigen excess; both can cause false-negative results.
A titre is the highest dilution giving a positive result; 1:160 means 1 part serum in 160 parts total.
ELISA uses an enzyme label and substrate; serology results are valid only when controls pass and reactive screens may need confirmation.

en.title: Haematology and blood banking
en.short: Blood cell formation, haemoglobin, counts, PCV, films, blood groups, compatibility and sample storage.

sections.heading: Blood cell formation
sections.text: Haematopoiesis is blood cell formation. In adults it occurs mainly in bone marrow, from stem cells that mature into red cells, white cells and platelets. Erythropoiesis, red cell making, is stimulated by erythropoietin, a hormone made mainly by the kidneys when oxygen is low. Leucopoiesis makes white cells for defence, and thrombopoiesis makes platelets for clotting. The fetal liver and spleen also make blood cells, but marrow takes over before birth.

sections.heading: Haemoglobin and counts
sections.text: Haemoglobin (Hb) is the red cell protein that carries oxygen. It has four globin chains, each with a haem group containing iron. Hb is measured in g/L or g/dL; anaemia means a low Hb for age and sex. A full blood count reports red cells, white cells, platelets and indices. Manual counts use a haemocytometer and dilution; automated analysers use impedance or light scatter. Report counts in cells per litre and use the laboratory reference range.

sections.heading: PCV and blood film
sections.text: Packed cell volume (PCV), or haematocrit, is the proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells after centrifugation. PCV = height of red cell column ÷ total column × 100. If red cells are 45 mm and the total is 100 mm, PCV = 45 ÷ 100 × 100 = 45%, or 0.45 L/L. A blood film is a thin blood layer on a slide, stained with a Romanowsky stain. It shows red cell shape, size and colour, white cell types and platelets. A good film is well spread, not too thick.

sections.heading: Groups and banking
sections.text: ABO groups depend on A and B antigens on red cells and anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma. Rh D is the main Rh antigen; D-negative people can make anti-D. Compatibility testing includes ABO and Rh D grouping, an antibody screen and a crossmatch before transfusion. Safe sample handling means correct labelling, the right tube, gentle mixing and prompt processing. Store samples and blood components only at temperatures stated in the local standard operating procedure and national blood service guidelines.

keyPoints: Haematopoiesis occurs mainly in bone marrow in adults and is regulated by hormones such as erythropoietin.
Haemoglobin is a tetramer with haem groups, and anaemia is a low haemoglobin for age and sex.
PCV = red cell column height ÷ total column height × 100.
For a 0.1 mm deep counting chamber, cells/L = average count per 1 mm² square × dilution × 10⁷.
ABO and Rh D grouping, an antibody screen and a crossmatch are part of compatibility testing before transfusion.
Handle samples with correct labelling, tube type, gentle mixing and validated storage temperatures, following local and national rules.

en.title: Histology and cytology techniques
en.short: Tissue fixation, processing, sectioning, H&E staining, microscopy and cytological smears.

sections.heading: Fixation and processing
sections.text: Fixation treats tissue with a chemical such as neutral buffered formalin to preserve structure and stop autolysis (self-digestion) and putrefaction. It hardens the tissue and stabilises proteins. After fixation, dehydration removes water through graded ethanol, because wax is not miscible with water. Clearing replaces the alcohol with a fluid such as xylene that is miscible with both alcohol and melted paraffin; the tissue often becomes translucent. These steps are called tissue processing.

sections.heading: Embedding and sectioning
sections.text: Embedding places the cleared tissue in melted paraffin wax, which sets into a block and supports the tissue for cutting. A microtome cuts thin sections, commonly 3 to 5 µm for routine paraffin work. The block is trimmed before cutting. The section is floated on warm water, picked onto a glass slide and dried. Poor dehydration or clearing leaves milky wax or crumbly sections. Section thickness affects staining and detail.

sections.heading: Staining and microscopy
sections.text: Routine staining uses haematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Haematoxylin stains nuclei blue to purple; eosin stains cytoplasm and collagen pink. Staining is not the same as fixation: it gives contrast, not preservation. Under a brightfield microscope, total magnification is objective magnification × eyepiece magnification. A 40× objective with a 10× eyepiece gives 400×. Resolution, not magnification, limits fine detail; magnifying beyond the resolution limit gives empty magnification.

sections.heading: Cytology smears
sections.text: Cytology examines individual cells, often shed or scraped, rather than tissue architecture. A cytological smear is spread thinly on a slide and fixed immediately, usually in 95% ethanol for Pap (Papanicolaou) staining, or air-dried for Giemsa-type stains. A case: a cervical scrape is spread, wet-fixed, stained by Pap and screened for abnormal cells. Smears need even thickness and rapid fixation to prevent drying artefact.

keyPoints: Fixation preserves tissue by stopping autolysis and putrefaction, usually with neutral buffered formalin.
Dehydration uses graded ethanol; clearing uses a fluid miscible with alcohol and paraffin, such as xylene.
Embedding supports tissue in paraffin; a microtome cuts routine sections commonly 3 to 5 µm thick.
In H&E, haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple and eosin stains cytoplasm and collagen pink.
Total microscope magnification = objective magnification × eyepiece magnification; 40× with 10× gives 400×.
Cytological smears examine individual cells and need thin spreading and prompt fixation to avoid drying artefact.

en.title: Parasitology and medical entomology
en.short: Collecting and examining parasite specimens, common protozoa and helminths, medical vectors and safe handling.

sections.heading: Specimen collection
sections.text: Parasitology identifies parasites in stool, urine, blood and sputum. Collect the right specimen at the right time: fresh stool for motile feeding forms, urine for Schistosoma haematobium eggs, and thick and thin blood films for malaria. Label every container, record clinical details, and send specimens promptly. Preserve only when delay is unavoidable; fixatives and transport media vary, so follow the local procedure. Stool must not be contaminated with urine.

sections.heading: Microscopy and parasites
sections.text: A wet mount, a drop of specimen on a slide under a cover slip, is examined promptly for motile protozoa (single-celled parasites) and eggs. Concentration methods such as formol-ether sedimentation increase recovery of cysts (resting forms) and eggs. Giemsa-stained blood films show Plasmodium and trypanosomes; modified acid-fast staining shows Cryptosporidium. The Scotch tape test collects Enterobius vermicularis eggs from perianal skin. Common protozoa include Plasmodium, Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia duodenalis and Trichomonas vaginalis. Common helminths (parasitic worms) include Ascaris lumbricoides, hookworm, Schistosoma species, Taenia species and Wuchereria bancrofti. Case: Amina has bloody diarrhoea; stool microscopy shows Entamoeba histolytica feeding forms and cysts.

sections.heading: Vectors and insects
sections.text: A vector is an organism that transmits a pathogen from one host to another. Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria; Aedes aegypti transmits dengue and yellow fever; Culex mosquitoes transmit filariasis. Glossina tsetse flies transmit African trypanosomiasis; Simulium blackflies transmit onchocerciasis; phlebotomine sandflies transmit leishmaniasis. Fleas, ticks and lice also transmit disease. Identify vectors by body shape and breeding sites, and record place and date of collection. Control relies on reducing breeding sites, personal protection and approved insecticides.

sections.heading: Safe handling
sections.text: Treat all specimens as potentially infectious. Wear gloves, a laboratory coat and eye protection. Do not eat, drink or mouth pipette. Work in a biological safety cabinet when aerosols are likely. Disinfect benches before and after work, autoclave waste, and put sharps in a puncture-resistant container. Clean spills with absorbent material and a suitable disinfectant. Formalin is toxic, so use it in a ventilated area. Report exposures at once and follow local biosafety rules.

keyPoints: Collect fresh, correctly labelled specimens at the right time and send them promptly.
Wet mounts and concentration methods detect protozoan cysts and helminth eggs; stained films are needed for blood parasites.
Common protozoa include Plasmodium, Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia duodenalis and Trichomonas vaginalis.
Common helminths include Ascaris lumbricoides, hookworm, Schistosoma species and Taenia species.
Vectors include Anopheles, Aedes, Culex, Glossina, Simulium and phlebotomine sandflies.
Treat every specimen as infectious: use gloves, a laboratory coat, eye protection and safe waste disposal.

en.title: Environmental and water analysis
en.short: Sampling water, soil and air, then pH, conductivity, DO, BOD, COD, hardness, nutrients, metals and standards.

sections.heading: Sampling and field checks
sections.text:
Representative sampling comes first. For water, rinse the container with the sample, fill it with no headspace for oxygen tests, and preserve or analyse it within the holding time. For soil, take a composite of several cores from the same depth and mix them. For air, draw a known volume through a filter or adsorbent tube at a measured flow rate.

Measure pH and dissolved oxygen (DO) in the field. pH is −log10 of hydrogen ion activity; calibrate the meter with two buffers. Conductivity measures the ability of water to carry current through dissolved ions, in µS/cm, and rises with ionic concentration. DO is the oxygen dissolved in water, in mg/L, and falls as temperature rises.

sections.heading: Oxygen demand
sections.text:
Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) is the oxygen used by microbes to break down organic matter, usually over five days at 20 °C (BOD5). Chemical oxygen demand (COD) is the oxygen equivalent of matter oxidised by a strong chemical oxidant, commonly acid dichromate. COD is faster and includes non-biodegradable matter; BOD reflects what microbes can degrade.

Example: a sample is diluted 1:20, so the dilution factor is 20. Initial DO = 8.4 mg/L; final DO after five days = 3.2 mg/L.
BOD5 = (8.4 − 3.2) × 20 = 5.2 × 20 = 104 mg/L.
If seeded dilution water is used, subtract the seed correction.

sections.heading: Hardness, nutrients and metals
sections.text:
Hardness is mainly calcium and magnesium, reported as mg/L CaCO3 and measured by EDTA titration. Nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate are measured colorimetrically or by ion chromatography; excess phosphate and nitrate can cause eutrophication, with excess plant growth and oxygen loss.

Heavy metals (for example lead, cadmium, mercury) are measured by atomic absorption spectroscopy or inductively coupled plasma (ICP) techniques. Results are compared with the relevant standard: drinking-water guidelines, irrigation limits or effluent limits. Standards differ by country and use, so quote the current national standard or WHO guideline and state the sample type and units.

keyPoints: Take representative samples; preserve them and analyse within the holding time.
pH = −log10 a(H+); conductivity in µS/cm indicates dissolved ions; DO in mg/L falls as temperature rises.
BOD5 = (D1 − D2) × dilution factor, where D1 and D2 are initial and final dissolved oxygen.
COD uses acid dichromate and is faster than BOD but includes non-biodegradable matter.
Total hardness is reported as mg/L CaCO3 and measured by EDTA titration.
Compare results with the current national standard or WHO guideline for the intended use, stating units and sample type.

en.title: Industrial, food and product analysis
en.short: This summary covers identity, purity, strength and quality tests, plus moisture, ash, fat, protein, pH and viscosity.

sections.heading: Identity and purity
sections.text: Product analysis starts with a specification: the written list of identity, purity, strength and quality that a material must meet. Identity confirms that a raw material is the named substance, not a substitute. Purity measures unwanted matter such as water, ash, heavy metals or solvent residues. Strength, or assay, measures how much active ingredient is present. Quality covers appearance, colour, odour, texture and performance. Laboratories use official methods published by bodies such as AOAC International, ISO or the relevant pharmacopoeia; these methods differ by product and country, so use the current edition named in the specification.

sections.heading: Moisture, ash, fat, protein
sections.text:
Moisture is water content, usually found by drying to constant mass. Ash is the mineral residue left after burning off organic matter. Fat is extracted with a solvent such as petroleum ether, then weighed after solvent removal. Protein is often estimated from nitrogen by the Kjeldahl method; percentage protein = percentage nitrogen × factor. The factor is 6.25 for many foods but differs for others, so check the official method.

Example: a 5.000 g food sample dries to 4.250 g.
Moisture = (5.000 − 4.250) ÷ 5.000 × 100 = 15.0%.
Ash = mass of ash ÷ mass of sample × 100.

sections.heading: pH, viscosity and strength
sections.text: pH measures acidity: pH = −log10[H+], where [H+] is hydrogen ion concentration in mol/L. A pH meter must be calibrated with buffers before use. Viscosity measures resistance to flow; it depends on temperature and concentration, so report the test conditions. In drugs, cosmetics and industrial products, routine tests also include density, refractive index, colour, odour and active-ingredient assay. Results are compared with the specification, and the sample is accepted only if every test passes. Record raw data and conditions so another analyst can repeat the work.

keyPoints: A specification states the identity, purity, strength and quality a material must meet.
Moisture % = (initial mass − dry mass) ÷ initial mass × 100.
Ash % = mass of ash ÷ mass of sample × 100.
Protein % is often nitrogen % × a factor; 6.25 is common for many foods but not universal.
pH = −log10[H+] and viscosity must be reported with temperature and concentration.
Use the current official method and specification for the product and country, because methods differ.

en.title: Quality assurance, method validation and accreditation
en.short: QC charts, SOPs, calibration, validation, uncertainty, proficiency testing, audits and accreditation.

sections.heading: Quality control charts
sections.text:
Quality control (QC) checks whether a method is performing as expected while routine samples are tested. A control chart plots repeated measurements of a stable control material against time. The centre line is the established mean. Control limits are commonly the mean ± 3 standard deviations (SD), and warning limits are mean ± 2SD. A point outside a control limit, or a trend, signals a problem to investigate before results are released.

For example, if a control material has mean 100 and SD 2, the control limits are 94 and 106. A result of 107 is outside the upper limit, so the run is rejected and cause is sought.

sections.heading: Calibration and validation
sections.text:
An SOP (standard operating procedure) is a written, approved instruction for a task, so that trained staff perform it the same way. Calibration compares an instrument’s response with a reference standard of known value and adjusts it if needed. The reference must be traceable through an unbroken chain to a national or international standard.

Validation confirms that a method is fit for its intended use. It examines accuracy, precision, specificity, linearity, range, limit of detection, limit of quantification and robustness. Measurement uncertainty is the range within which the true value is expected to lie. It combines contributions from sampling, standards, instruments, operators and random variation. Results should be reported with an uncertainty statement when required.

sections.heading: Proficiency testing and accreditation
sections.text:
Proficiency testing (PT) sends unknown samples to several laboratories and compares their results. A score is z = (x − assigned value) ÷ standard deviation, where the assigned value is the target value set by the PT provider. A large z value, |z| > 3, prompts investigation. Internal audits are planned checks by trained staff against the laboratory’s own procedures and a standard such as ISO/IEC 17025.

Accreditation is formal recognition by an independent national accreditation body that a laboratory is competent for defined tests. It supports confidence, comparability and trade. Accreditation bodies and rules vary by country, so check the current national body and standard edition.

keyPoints: Control charts usually use a centre line at the mean and control limits at mean ± 3SD, with warning limits at mean ± 2SD.
An SOP is an approved written procedure that makes a task repeatable.
Calibration must be traceable to a reference standard; validation shows a method is fit for purpose.
Measurement uncertainty combines relevant sources of uncertainty and is often reported as expanded uncertainty U = k × u, with k = 2 giving about 95% coverage for a normal distribution.
Proficiency testing compares a laboratory with peers, often using a z-score such as z = (x − assigned value) ÷ SD.
Internal audits check compliance, while accreditation is independent recognition of competence, commonly against ISO/IEC 17025.

en.title: Laboratory management, professional practice and ethics
en.short: Running a laboratory: organisation, stock control, roles, ethics, records, waste and emergencies.

sections.heading: Organisation and roles
sections.text: A laboratory is organised as a chain of responsibility. The laboratory manager sets policy and staffing. A technical manager controls methods and equipment; a quality manager runs audits; a safety officer coordinates risk control. Bench staff include analysts, technicians and assistants. An organisation chart and procedures show who approves, performs and checks work. Maintenance is planned: each instrument has a schedule, service log and rule for taking it out of service when faulty.

sections.heading: Stock control
sections.text: Inventory and stock control keep enough consumables and reagents without waste. A stock card records receipts, issues, balances and expiry dates. Set a reorder level and safety stock. Use first in, first out, or first expiry, first out for perishables. Reorder point = average daily use × lead time in days + safety stock. Example: use 20 units a day, lead time 10 days, safety stock 50 units. Reorder point = 20 × 10 + 50 = 250 units.

sections.heading: Ethics and records
sections.text: Professional codes require honesty, competence, impartiality and confidentiality. Staff must report results truthfully, declare conflicts of interest and work within their competence. Confidential information should be shared only with authorised people. Data protection and laboratory laws differ by country, so check national rules. Records must be legible, dated, traceable to the person who made them, and kept secure. Retention periods vary by record type and country. Regulatory responsibilities include registration, accreditation and reporting. ISO/IEC 17025 is an international standard for testing and calibration laboratories; accreditation is voluntary in many countries.

sections.heading: Waste and emergencies
sections.text: Waste handling is a management duty. Segregate waste at the point of use into labelled containers, follow local rules for chemical, biological and sharps waste, and use licensed carriers. Keep disposal records. Emergency planning covers fire, chemical spill, injury, power failure and loss of containment. The plan names who does what, lists contacts and sets evacuation routes. Test it with drills and review it after incidents. Requirements differ by country and institution, so confirm them with the regulator.

keyPoints: A laboratory needs a clear chain of responsibility and written procedures for approval, performance and checking of work.
Maintenance schedules and service logs keep instruments traceable and allow faulty equipment to be taken out of service.
Reorder point = average daily use × lead time in days + safety stock; use FIFO or FEFO for perishables.
Professional codes require honesty, competence, impartiality and confidentiality; staff must work within their competence.
Records must be legible, dated, traceable and secure; retention periods and data protection rules vary by country.
Waste must be segregated and disposed of under local rules, and emergency plans should be drilled and reviewed.

en.title: Research methods and the final-year project
en.short: Choosing a problem, literature search, design, sampling, statistics, ethics, proposal, records and defence.

sections.heading: From idea to proposal
sections.text:
Choose a problem that is specific, feasible and ethical. Read review articles first, then primary papers, and record every source you use. A proposal states the aim, objectives, background, methods, materials, timeline, risks and budget.

Keep a laboratory notebook: date each entry, write the aim, method, raw data and any deviation, and never erase errors.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text:
