Experimental design means planning treatments, controls, replication and randomisation so that a real effect can be separated from chance. A control is a comparison group; replication repeats the measurement; randomisation reduces bias.

Sampling starts with a clear population. In probability sampling every unit has a known chance of selection; convenience sampling does not, so it limits generalisation. Sample size depends on variability, the smallest effect worth detecting and statistical power (the chance of detecting a real effect). Check your department’s guidance.

sections.heading: Statistics and ethics
sections.text:
Summarise data with the mean and standard deviation (SD). Mean is average; SD measures spread. For two groups, a t-test compares means when data are roughly normal; otherwise use a non-parametric test. Report sample size n, mean, SD and p-value. A p-value is the probability of data, or more extreme data, if the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

Example: lead in water, mg/L: 0.10, 0.12, 0.14, 0.16, 0.18, 0.20. Mean = 0.90 ÷ 6 = 0.15. Deviations from 0.15 are −0.05, −0.03, −0.01, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05. Squares sum to 0.0070. Sample variance = 0.0070 ÷ 5 = 0.0014, so SD = √0.0014 = 0.037 mg/L.

Ethics: obtain informed consent for human participants, guardian consent for minors, and ethics committee approval. Keep data confidential. Never fabricate or alter results. Rules vary by country.

sections.heading: Report and defence
sections.text:
Write the report with title, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Use past tense for what you did.

In the oral defence, explain why you chose each method, your sample size and limitations. Rehearse, keep slides simple, and answer honestly; say when you do not know.

keyPoints: A good project problem is specific, feasible and ethical; the proposal states aim, methods, timeline and risks.
Experimental design uses controls, replication and randomisation to separate real effects from chance.
Probability sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection; convenience sampling limits generalisation.
Mean = Σx ÷ n and sample standard deviation = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)).
A p-value is the probability of the data if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
Keep dated raw records, write the report in the standard order, obtain consent and ethics approval where needed, and defend your design and limitations.

en.title: Advanced analytical chemistry and trace analysis
en.short: Advanced spectroscopy, hyphenated methods, trace sample preparation, validation, detection limits and uncertainty.

sections.heading: Hyphenated methods
sections.text: Trace analysis measures an analyte (the substance sought) at low concentration in a matrix (the rest of the sample). Hyphenated techniques couple two methods, usually a separation with a detector: GC-MS, LC-MS/MS and ICP-MS. Separation reduces matrix interference; detection identifies and quantifies. MS/MS selects a precursor ion and fragments it, giving high selectivity. High-resolution MS measures exact mass. Isotope dilution uses a known amount of an isotopically labelled analogue as an internal standard (a known added compound); it compensates for recovery and ionisation changes.

sections.heading: Trace sample preparation
sections.text: Sample preparation is often the largest error source. The aim is to isolate the analyte and remove matrix without loss or contamination. Techniques include liquid-liquid extraction, solid-phase extraction (SPE), headspace and purge-and-trap for volatiles, and acid digestion for metals. Use clean reagents, blanks, and certified reference materials (CRMs). Preconcentration lowers the limit of detection but can also concentrate interferents. Recovery is checked by spiking a blank or sample.

sections.heading: Method development and validation
sections.text: Method development fixes selectivity (freedom from interference), calibration range, sample size and internal standard. Validation then shows fitness for purpose through accuracy, precision, recovery, linearity, robustness and carry-over (residue from a previous sample). Acceptance criteria must be set before experiments. For trace methods, batch quality control includes reagent blanks, method blanks, duplicates and spiked samples.

sections.heading: Detection limits and uncertainty
sections.text: The limit of detection (LOD) is the lowest amount that can be detected with stated confidence; the limit of quantification (LOQ) is the lowest amount that can be measured with acceptable precision. A common approach uses LOD = 3.3s ÷ S and LOQ = 10s ÷ S, where s is the standard deviation of low-level response and S is the calibration slope. State the definition used. Measurement uncertainty combines all sources: u = √(Σu_i²), expanded U = k u, usually k = 2 for about 95% confidence. Example: S = 2500 counts per µg/L, s = 12 counts. LOD = 3.3 × 12 ÷ 2500 = 0.0158 µg/L (15.8 ng/L); LOQ = 10 × 12 ÷ 2500 = 0.048 µg/L.

keyPoints: Hyphenated techniques combine two methods, usually a separation with selective detection, such as GC-MS, LC-MS/MS and ICP-MS.
Isotope dilution and internal standards correct for recovery and signal variation.
Trace sample preparation must control contamination, losses and matrix effects using blanks and certified reference materials.
Validation parameters include selectivity, linearity, accuracy, precision, recovery and robustness.
LOD = 3.3s ÷ S and LOQ = 10s ÷ S, with definitions stated.
Combined standard uncertainty u = √(Σu_i²) and expanded uncertainty U = k u.

en.title: Molecular biology and biotechnology techniques
en.short: Nucleic acid extraction, PCR, electrophoresis, blotting, sequencing, cell culture, biosafety and applications.

sections.heading: Extraction and PCR
sections.text:
Nucleic acid extraction releases DNA or RNA from cells, removes proteins and lipids, and inactivates nucleases, nucleic-acid-degrading enzymes. Methods use phenol and chloroform, silica columns or magnetic beads. RNA work needs RNase-free conditions; RNA is usually converted to complementary DNA before PCR.

PCR, the polymerase chain reaction, copies a target sequence exponentially. A reaction contains template, two primers, deoxynucleotides, a heat-stable DNA polymerase and buffer with magnesium ions. Cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension double the target each time. Ideally, n cycles give 2ⁿ copies: 20 cycles give 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 copies. Real efficiency is lower.

sections.heading: Separation and blotting
sections.text:
Electrophoresis separates charged molecules in a gel under an electric field. DNA and RNA are usually run in agarose; proteins and small fragments use polyacrylamide. Nucleic acids carry negative charge and move towards the anode. Smaller fragments travel faster, so bands are compared with a size ladder. The gel is stained and viewed.

Blotting transfers separated molecules to a membrane for detection. Southern blotting detects DNA, Northern blotting detects RNA and Western blotting detects protein with antibodies.

sections.heading: Sequencing and culture
sections.text:
Sequencing determines the order of nucleotides. Sanger sequencing uses chain-terminating dideoxynucleotides, producing fragments of different lengths that are separated and read. Next-generation sequencing reads many DNA molecules in parallel, giving large data sets requiring bioinformatics.

Cell culture grows cells outside the body under sterile conditions. Mammalian cells are kept at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% carbon dioxide. Medium supplies nutrients and controls pH. Cells are passaged when confluent, and contamination must be monitored.

sections.heading: Biosafety and uses
sections.text:
Biosafety means containment practices that prevent exposure and release. Work is classified by risk group and containment level, following national rules and guidance such as the WHO Laboratory Biosafety Manual. Aseptic technique, training, waste inactivation and controlled access are central.

Molecular methods support diagnosis of infections and genetic disorders, typing of organisms, food and environmental testing, and research on gene expression and cell function. Results depend on controls and validated methods.

keyPoints: Nucleic acid extraction must remove proteins and nucleases; RNA work needs RNase-free conditions and often reverse transcription.
PCR uses primers, heat-stable polymerase and cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension; ideal yield is 2ⁿ copies after n cycles.
Electrophoresis separates nucleic acids by size and charge, usually in agarose, and is checked against a size ladder.
Southern, Northern and Western blotting detect DNA, RNA and protein respectively after transfer to a membrane.
Sanger sequencing reads chain-terminating fragments; next-generation sequencing reads many molecules in parallel.
Cell culture needs sterile technique, suitable medium and controlled temperature and carbon dioxide; biosafety follows risk group and containment rules.

en.title: Advanced biomedical laboratory science
en.short: Advanced clinical chemistry, haematology, microbiology, diagnostic algorithms, QC and result interpretation.

sections.heading: Clinical chemistry and haematology
sections.text: Advanced clinical chemistry measures analytes such as electrolytes, enzymes, hormones and biomarkers. Haematology covers full blood counts, blood film morphology and coagulation. Results are interpreted against age- and sex-related reference intervals, previous results (delta check) and the clinical picture. A critical value is a result suggesting immediate danger, such as severe hypoglycaemia or a very low platelet count; it must be telephoned and documented promptly. Laboratories also verify that results fit the sample and method.

sections.heading: Microbiology and algorithms
sections.text: A diagnostic algorithm is an ordered decision path: history, pretest probability, screening test, then confirmatory test. In microbiology, microscopy, culture, antigen and molecular tests are chosen by suspected organism and urgency. Sensitivity is true positives ÷ (true positives + false negatives); specificity is true negatives ÷ (true negatives + false positives). Predictive values depend on prevalence, so a good test in one population may mislead in another. Sequential testing, where a second test is done only after a positive first test, raises specificity and positive predictive value but lowers sensitivity. Antimicrobial susceptibility results guide safe therapy.

sections.heading: Quality control
sections.text: Internal quality control uses stable control materials with an established mean and standard deviation (SD), plotted on a Levey-Jennings chart. Westgard rules flag random and systematic error; for example, a 1-3s rule rejects a run when one control exceeds mean ± 3 SD. External quality assessment compares the laboratory with peers. The coefficient of variation (CV) is SD ÷ mean × 100%. If a glucose control has mean 5.0 mmol/L and SD 0.2 mmol/L, CV = 0.2 ÷ 5.0 × 100% = 4.0%. A control result of 5.7 mmol/L is (5.7 − 5.0) ÷ 0.2 = 3.5 SD from the mean, so the run is rejected under 1-3s.

sections.heading: Supporting disease management
sections.text: Laboratories support management by monitoring treatment, reporting turnaround time and notifying critical results. Interpretive comments should state limitations and suggest confirmatory testing. Clinicians and laboratory staff share responsibility for using results with the patient’s history and examination.

keyPoints: Interpret results against reference intervals, previous results and clinical context, and report critical values urgently.
Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN); specificity = TN ÷ (TN + FP).
Predictive values depend on disease prevalence, so test performance varies between populations.
Sequential testing raises specificity and positive predictive value but lowers sensitivity.
Internal QC uses Levey-Jennings charts and Westgard rules; CV = SD ÷ mean × 100%.
A control result beyond mean ± 3 SD is rejected under the 1-3s rule.

en.title: Advanced research methods and postgraduate dissertation
en.short: Research design, systematic review, statistics, ethics, data management, thesis writing and defence.

sections.heading: Design and review
sections.text:
Research design is the plan linking question, variables, sample and analysis. Choose it before collecting data: experimental, observational, survey or qualitative, with a sampling strategy and stated limitations.

A systematic literature review uses a focused question, explicit search terms, inclusion and exclusion criteria and a record of decisions, so another person can repeat it. It differs from a narrative review because it is protocol-led and transparent.

sections.heading: Statistics and data
sections.text:
Match the model to the design: t-tests and analysis of variance compare group means; regression describes relationships. Check assumptions and report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not p-values alone. A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis (no real difference) is true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

Example: two groups of 25, means 12.4 and 10.8, pooled standard deviation 2.0.
t = (12.4 − 10.8) ÷ (2.0 × √(2/25)) = 1.6 ÷ 0.566 = 2.83
With 48 degrees of freedom the two-sided p-value is about 0.007.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text:
Research ethics covers informed consent, confidentiality, risk to participants, animal welfare and honest reporting. Most institutions require ethics approval before recruitment; rules vary by country and institution, so check the current local policy.

Data management means planning how data are collected, labelled, stored, backed up, shared and destroyed. A data management plan names formats, access controls and retention periods. Keep raw data and analysis scripts so results can be reproduced.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text: The dissertation reports background, methods, results and discussion in a clear structure, with figures and tables that stand alone. The defence (viva voce) is an oral examination: explain your choices, defend your interpretation and state limits honestly.

keyPoints: Fix the research design before collecting data.
A systematic review is protocol-led and repeatable.
Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not p-values alone.
A p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
Ethics approval comes before recruitment; rules vary by country.
Keep raw data and analysis scripts so work can be reproduced.
